title: Act I, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: On the heath the Witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor and 'king hereafter', and tell Banquo he will 'get kings, though thou be none.' They vanish. Ross and Angus arrive to tell Macbeth he is now Thane of Cawdor. Macbeth, startled, imagines murder ('horrible imaginings') and decides 'chance may crown me'; Banquo warns that 'instruments of darkness tell us truths' to betray us.

context.history: Prophecy was a dangerous subject: predicting a monarch's death could be treason. Banquo's line about 'instruments of darkness' reflects the period's belief that the devil tells half-truths to trap souls.

significance: The scene splits two responses to the same temptation: Banquo is wary, Macbeth is already thinking of murder. Whether the prophecy causes the crime or reveals a desire already there is the play's central question about fate and free will.

segments.script: Prophecy was a dangerous subject: predicting a monarch's death could be treason. Banquo's line about 'instruments of darkness' reflects the period's belief that the devil tells half-truths to trap souls. The scene splits two responses to the same temptation: Banquo is wary, Macbeth is already thinking of murder. Whether the prophecy causes the crime or reveals a desire already there is the play's central question about fate and free will. Characterization: Macbeth "starts" at the prophecy; Banquo is wary ("instruments of darkness"). Macbeth's asides reveal that he is already imagining murder. Dramatic irony: The audience knows Macbeth is Cawdor before he does; the prophecy's first part comes true at once. Diction / vocabulary: Macbeth's first line echoes the witches: "So foul and fair a day I have not seen." Watch for the prophecies: The witches' riddling prophecies (Birnam Wood, no man of woman born) feed Macbeth's false confidence and then destroy it. In this scene: “Good sir, why do you start; and seem to fear / Things that do sound so fair? I’ the name of truth” (Act I, Scene III, Banquo).
